stem: When reviewing pretransplant immunization needs for an adult transplant candidate, in which situation is rabies vaccination among the recommended adult candidate immunizations?

options.text: Exposure or potential exposure due to vocation
Routine administration to every candidate regardless of risk
Only after transplantation when live vaccines are preferred
Only for pediatric candidates younger than 9 years

explanation.rationale_correct: Recommended pretransplant adult immunizations include rabies vaccination for exposure or potential exposures due to vocations only, rather than universal routine administration.

rationale_incorrect.B: Rabies vaccine is listed for vocation-related exposure risk, not for every candidate by default.
rationale_incorrect.C: Pretransplant immunization guidance emphasizes updating vaccines before transplant; live vaccines require careful post-transplant timing.
rationale_incorrect.D: The cited rabies recommendation is within adult candidate immunizations, not limited to young pediatric candidates.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → Immunizations → B. Recommended Pretransplant Immunizations → 1.a.i.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Rabies (exposure or potential exposures due to vocations only)

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 5 → Immunizations → B.1.a.i. (rabies for vocation-related exposure); PDF p. 180 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Rabies-vaccination indication angle distinct from general pretransplant vaccine-response teaching (cctc-1081) and live-vaccine interval (cctc-1077); anchor verified on Cupples p. 180.

stem: A coordinator is counseling an adolescent solid-organ transplant recipient about sexual health and immunizations. Which teaching point aligns with standard references?

options.text: Pediatric recipients should receive HPV and hepatitis B vaccine before engaging in sexual activity
Post-transplant recipients never need HPV or hepatitis B vaccination
Live-virus vaccines are preferred immediately after transplant for all adolescents
Sexual-health counseling is deferred until 5 years after transplantation

explanation.rationale_correct: Sexual-health education for pediatric recipients includes that they should receive HPV and hepatitis B vaccine prior to engaging in sexual activity.

rationale_incorrect.B: HPV and hepatitis B vaccination remain important preventive measures for pediatric recipients.
rationale_incorrect.C: Live vaccines require careful timing after transplantation rather than being preferred immediately.
rationale_incorrect.D: Sexual-health and vaccination counseling is part of ongoing education rather than deferred for years.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → sexual health → ix.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Pediatric recipients should receive the HPV and hepatitis B vaccine prior to engaging in sexual activity

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → sexual health → ix. (pediatric HPV and hepatitis B before sexual activity); PDF p. 121 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Sixteenth pediatric recipient in bank; sexual-health vaccination angle distinct from pediatric HPV-only teaching (cctc-1036) and community-infection severity (cctc-1056); anchor verified on Cupples p. 121.

stem: A coordinator is updating adenovirus infection-prevention teaching for solid-organ transplant recipients. Evaluate the following statements:

elements.text: Adenoviruses may cause respiratory, gastrointestinal, conjunctival, or disseminated pathology in solid-organ transplant recipients.
Adenovirus infections are most common in the first 3 months after transplant and with higher immunosuppression dosing.
Adenovirus infection is limited exclusively to kidney transplant recipients.
Adenovirus never causes gastrointestinal pathology in transplant recipients.

explanation.rationale_correct: Adenoviruses may cause respiratory, GI, conjunctival, or disseminated disease in solid-organ recipients and are most common early post-transplant with higher immunosuppression. They are not kidney-specific and may cause GI pathology, so statements III and IV are false.

rationale_incorrect.B: Statement IV is false because GI pathology is among the described adenovirus manifestations.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statements I and II are true; statements III and IV are false.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statements III and IV are false.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → CARV → 11.a. Adenoviruses → i.–iii.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: respiratory, GI, conjunctival, and disseminated pathology … Most common in the first 3 months … higher immunosuppression dosing

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 5 → CARV → 11.a. Adenoviruses → i.–iii. (respiratory, GI, conjunctival, and disseminated pathology range; most common in the first 3 months with higher immunosuppression dosing); PDF p. 211 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Adenovirus teaching combo distinct from parvovirus combo (cctc-1083) and JC virus combo (cctc-1079); anchor verified on Cupples p. 211.

stem: When teaching a recipient about human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) after transplantation, which timing statement aligns with standard references?

options.text: Onset typically occurs between 2 and 4 weeks posttransplantation
HHV-6 occurs only before the transplant operation
Onset is expected more than 1 year after every transplant
HHV-6 reactivation never coincides with CMV coinfection

explanation.rationale_correct: HHV-6 is usually reactivation of endogenous latent virus with onset typically between 2 and 4 weeks posttransplantation; CMV coinfection is common.

rationale_incorrect.B: HHV-6 disease is described as post-transplant reactivation rather than a preoperative-only process.
rationale_incorrect.C: Standard references describe onset in the early post-transplant weeks, not uniformly after 1 year.
rationale_incorrect.D: CMV coinfection with HHV-6 is described as common rather than absent.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → G. Human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) → 1.–3.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Usually reactivation … Onset typically occurs between 2 and 4 weeks posttransplantation … CMV coinfection is common

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 5 → G. HHV-6 → 1.–3. (reactivation, 2–4 week onset, CMV coinfection); PDF p. 203 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. HHV-6 education angle distinct from CMV organ-specific combo (cctc-1072) and EBV/PTLD screening (cctc-2071); anchor verified on Cupples p. 203.
